sections.h2: Can a squatter take ownership of a house in Michigan?
sections.html:
Only after holding the property openly, against the owner's rights, for the full statutory period, and then proving it in court. The period is 15 years in most cases. Moving into a vacant house does not create ownership in a month, a year or ten years.

Michigan has no separate squatter statute. The claim is adverse possession, which grows out of the limitation on actions to recover land in MCL 600.5801. When the time to sue for the land runs out, the owner loses the right to recover it.

Owners of vacant houses, inherited homes and rentals sitting empty between tenants are the most exposed. A long stretch without anyone checking the place is what gives an occupant the continuous years the claim needs. Walk the property, keep the taxes and utilities current in your own name, and give written permission where a neighbor uses a strip. All of that leaves a record that helps later.

An owner who acts early never reaches that point. Removing someone is quicker and cheaper in the first months than after years of acquiescence.

The statute sets the time within which a person must sue to recover land or enter it. The length depends on how the person in possession claims title.

Time limits to recover land under MCL 600.5801
How the occupant claims titleTime limit
Deed from an executor, administrator, guardian or testamentary trustee, from a sheriff or other officer under court process, or from a sheriff on a mortgage foreclosure sale5 years
Deed from an officer authorized to sell land for taxes10 years
A devise in a will15 years after the will is probated in Michigan
All other cases, including an occupant with no paper title15 years

A person with no deed at all, who simply moves in, falls in the last row. That is why 15 years is the figure most owners ask about.

sections.h2: What a claimant must prove in court
sections.html:
Michigan courts apply the same test in case after case. A claim requires clear and cogent proof that possession was actual, visible, open, notorious, exclusive, continuous and uninterrupted for the 15 years, and the burden of proof sits on the person who makes the claim.

  • Actual and visible: positive, affirmative acts of ownership, such as building, fencing, mowing or parking on the strip.
  • Open and notorious: so visible that the true owner is presumed to have notice, or the owner actually knew of the claim.
  • Hostile: use inconsistent with the owner's rights, without permission asked or given. It does not require ill will.
  • Exclusive and continuous: the claimant treated the land as their own to the exclusion of others for the full period, though constant use is not required and occasional trespasses by the owner do not defeat exclusivity.

Use with the owner's permission is not hostile, which is why a documented, revocable permission matters for a neighbor who has used part of a lot for years.

sections.h2: Combining years with a previous owner
sections.html:
A claimant can add years to an earlier occupant's years if the two were in privity. Successive periods can be joined, or tacked, to reach 15 years. In an unpublished Court of Appeals opinion from June 2023, a business owner and two earlier owners of the parcel were found to be in privity, which let their years of using a drive, a parking lot and a septic field be added together.

Privity can be shown by including the disputed land in the deed, or by an actual transfer of possession of the disputed strip through statements made at the time of the conveyance. This is a common source of disputes after a sale, because a buyer may find that the former owner's use of a strip has been counted toward a claim against the neighbor's lot.

Occasional entries do not. The period is interrupted only if the true owner reenters and stays in possession for at least one year, or files suit within one year of reentry (MCL 600.5868).

A quick fence-line walk or a chain across a driveway for a weekend leaves the clock running. An owner who suspects a claim should talk to a Michigan attorney about a lawsuit instead of relying on informal gestures.

A related doctrine, acquiescence, can fix a boundary line without proof of hostility. That claim needs only that the neighbors treated a boundary line or marker as the property line for 15 years, and the standard of proof is a preponderance of the evidence.

sections.h2: Removing someone who has no right to be there
sections.html:
Michigan allows summary proceedings to recover possession. Under MCL 600.5714(1)(f) a person entitled to possession can recover it from someone who took possession by forcible entry, holds by force after a peaceable entry, or came into possession by trespass without color of title or any other possessory interest.

Self-help is where owners get hurt. MCL 600.5711 bars entry unless the law permits it and, as a rule, requires a peaceable entry. Subsection (3) lets an owner enter without that limit when the occupant is a forcible-entry occupant or trespasser, but forcible entry does not include conduct covered by the assault chapter of the Michigan penal code.

Under MCL 600.2918, a person ejected by force is entitled to three times actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, plus possession, and a tenant can recover when an owner changes locks, removes doors, or cuts essential services. Subsection (5) provides that an owner does not unlawfully interfere with a trespasser who took possession by forcible entry or without color of title. If you are unsure whether the occupant is a tenant, treat them as one and use the eviction process.

sections.h2: If the occupant was once a tenant or guest
sections.html:
A former tenant or guest is not a trespasser. MCL 600.5714(1) gives separate routes for holding over after nonpayment of rent, for holding over after a lease ends, and for several other situations. For rent, the demand for possession gives the tenant 7 days to pay or leave.

If the owner's own title is clouded by someone else's long possession, the owner or the claimant can bring a quiet title action in circuit court under MCL 600.2932. Any person who claims a right in, or title to, land may sue anyone who claims an inconsistent interest, whether or not the defendant is in possession. These actions are equitable in nature.

sections.h2: Selling a house with an occupant problem
sections.html:
A squatter or a disputed strip complicates a listing, since a buyer's lender and title company will want the occupancy and the boundary settled before closing. Start by writing down what you know: when the occupant arrived, whether anyone ever gave permission, and what has been built or fenced on the land.

Then pick the route that fits the facts. An occupant who entered by trespass is a summary proceedings case. A former tenant needs the eviction process. A boundary dispute with a neighbor may need a quiet title action. Bring a Michigan attorney in early for any of these.

A cash buyer can often close with an occupant issue still open, because there is no lender waiting on a clean title commitment. The price will reflect the risk, and you still cannot lock anyone out by force, so settle the lawful route to possession first.

faqs.q: How many years until squatters have rights in Michigan?
faqs.a: Fifteen years in most cases under MCL 600.5801(4), and the claimant must still prove the elements by clear and cogent evidence. Shorter periods of 5 or 10 years apply when the occupant holds under certain court, sheriff or tax deeds.

faqs.q: Does paying the property taxes create ownership?
faqs.a: Tax payment is not one of the elements. The courts require possession that is actual, visible, open, notorious, exclusive, hostile and continuous for the full period.

faqs.q: Can I change the locks on a squatter?
faqs.a: Only with care. A lockout can be unlawful if the person is a tenant, and MCL 600.2918 allows triple damages for a forcible ejection. Use summary proceedings under MCL 600.5714(1)(f) when the occupant entered by trespass.

faqs.q: Is permission a defense to a claim?
faqs.a: Yes, in the sense that hostile use is use without permission asked or given. Written permission makes it harder for a neighbor to show the hostility the claim requires.

faqs.q: What deadline applies to a lawsuit for lockout damages?
faqs.a: A claim to regain possession must start within 90 days after the cause of action arises or becomes known, and a damages claim within one year, under MCL 600.2918(8).
